                  <ns0:p n="5">5 And the woman conceived, and sent, and told David, and said, I <ns0:hi>am</ns0:hi> with child <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">Consider therefore what to do for thy own honour, and for my safety, whom thou hast brought into a most shame<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ful and dangerous condition.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="6">6 And David sent to Joab, <ns0:hi>saying,</ns0:hi> Send me Uriah the Hittite: And Joab sent Uriah to Da<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vid.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="7">7 And when Uriah was come unto him, Da<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vid demanded <ns0:hi>of him</ns0:hi> 
                     <ns0:note n="‡" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> of the peace of, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note> how Joab did, and how the people did, and how the war prospered <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">Frivolous Questions which any common Messenger could have answered: which probably made <ns0:hi>Uriah</ns0:hi> suspect that there was some other secret cause why he was sent for. And he might understand something, either by <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi>'s Messengers, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 4. or by some of his own Family, concern<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing her being sent for to the Court: which together with other Circumstances might give him cause of further suspi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tion. Yet such might be the Questions (though not here par<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ticularly mentioned) concerning those Heads, as every pri<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vate person might not be acquainted with, nor able to resolve, but such onely as were acquainted with the Counsel of War.</ns0:note>?</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="8">8 And David said to Uriah, Go down to thy house <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">Not doubting but he would there Converse with his Wife, and so cover their Sin and Shame.</ns0:note>, and wash thy feet <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">As Travellers there used to do.</ns0:note>. And Uriah departed out of the kings house, and there <ns0:note n="‡" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> went out after him</ns0:note> followed him a mess <ns0:hi>of meat</ns0:hi> from the king <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">Seemingly as a Testimony of <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi>'s respect and Affection to him; but really to cheer up his Spirits, and dispose him to desire his Wives company.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="9">9 But Uriah slept at the door of the kings
<ns0:pb facs="tcp:107763:255" />
house with all the servants of his lord <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">With the King's Guard. This he did, either upon some suspition of the matter, See <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 7. Or, by the secret direction of Gods wise and irresistible Providence, who would bring <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi>'s Sin to light.</ns0:note>, and went not down to his house.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="10">10 And when they had told <ns0:note n="*" place="bottom">Whether of their own accord, or being first asked by <ns0:hi>David,</ns0:hi> it doth not appear.</ns0:note> David, saying, Uriah went not down unto his house, David said unto Uriah, Camest thou not from <ns0:hi>thy</ns0:hi> journey <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">Wearied with hard service and Travel, and therefore didst need refreshment; nor did I ex<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pect or desire that thou shouldest now attend upon my Person, or keep the Watch.</ns0:note>? why <ns0:hi>then</ns0:hi> didst thou not go down unto thine house?</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="11">11 And Uriah said unto David, The ark <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">Which it seems, was now carried with them for their encouragement and direction, as was usual: See <ns0:hi>Numb</ns0:hi> 10. 35. 1 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 4. 4.</ns0:note>, and Israel, and Judah abide in tents, and <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 20. 6.</ns0:note> my lord Joab, and the servants of my lord are en<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />camped in the open fields <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">To wit, in Tents which are in the Fields.</ns0:note>; shall I then go into mine house to eat, and to drink, and to lie with my wife <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">He might possibly add these words, to in<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sinuate his apprehension of the King's Design, and to awaken his Conscience to the consideration of his Sin, and of the Injury which he had done him. His meaning is, Now when God's People are in a doubtful and dangerous Condition, it becomes me to Sympathize with them, and to abstain even from lawful Delights. Whereby he might possibly in<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />timate, how unworthy it was for <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> in such a season to indulge himself in sinful and injurious Pleasures. But <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi>'s Ear was now Deaf, his Heart being hardned through the deceitfulness of Sin.</ns0:note>? <ns0:hi>As</ns0:hi> thou livest, and <ns0:hi>as</ns0:hi> thy soul liveth, I will not do this thing.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="12">12 And David said to Uriah, Tarry here to day also, and to morrow I will let thee depart. So Uriah abode in Jerusalem, that day and the mor<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />row.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="13">13 And when David had called him <ns0:note n="▪" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Being invited by <ns0:hi>David.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note>, he did eat and drink before him, and he made him drunk <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>he made him mer<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ry,</ns0:hi> as the Word oft signifies. He caused him to Drink more than was convenient.</ns0:note>: and at even he went out to lie on his bed <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">Which it doth not appear, that he did the Night before; but now his Excess in Eating and Drinking, might make it more necessary for him.</ns0:note> with the servants of his lord <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> In some Chamber in the King's Court, where the Kings Ser<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vants used to take their Repose.</ns0:note>, but went not down to his house.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="14">14 And it came to pass in the morning, that David wrote a letter to Joab, and sent <ns0:hi>it</ns0:hi> by the hand of Uriah.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="15">15 And he wrote in the letter, saying, Set ye Uriah in the forefront of the <ns0:note n="‡" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> strong.</ns0:note> hottest battel, and retire ye <ns0:note n="‡" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> from af<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ter him.</ns0:note> from him, that he may be smitten and die <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">So far is <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> from Repenting upon these just and great Occasions, that he seeks to cover one Sin with ano<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther; and to hide his Adultery with Murder, even the Mur<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />der of a most Excellent Person, and that in a most Malici<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ous and Perfidious manner.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="16">16 And it came to pass when Joab observed the city, that he assigned Uriah unto a place where he knew that valiant men <ns0:hi>were</ns0:hi> 
                     <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">Placed there to defend it, because that part of the City was supposed either the weakest, or the place designed for the Assault. <ns0:hi>Ioab</ns0:hi> having formerly committed a base Mur<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />der upon <ns0:hi>Abner,</ns0:hi> was ready to execute this wicked Com<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mand of the King; that so he being involved in the same Guilt with him, might the more willingly receive him into favour.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="17">17 And the men of the city went out and fought with Joab: and there fell some of the people of the servants of David, and Uriah the Hittite died also.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="18">18 Then Joab sent, and told David all the things concerning the war:</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="19">19 And charged the messenger, saying, When thou hast made an end of telling the matters of the war unto the king;</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="20">20 And if so be that the kings wrath arise, and he say unto thee, Wherefore approached ye so nigh unto the city when ye did fight? knew ye not that they would shoot from the wall?</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="21">21 Who smote <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Judg. 9. 53</ns0:note> Abimelech the son of Jerub<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />besheth? <ns0:note n="▪" place="bottom">Called also <ns0:hi>Ierubbaal, Iudg.</ns0:hi> 9. 1. See the note on 2 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 2. 8.</ns0:note> did not a woman cast a piece of a mil<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stone upon him from the wall, that he died in The<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bez? why went ye nigh the wall? then say thou, Thy servant Uriah the Hittite is dead also <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">Which he knew would be acceptable news to the King, and therefore allay his Wrath. This indeed might make the Messenger suspect that <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> had an hand in <ns0:hi>Uriah</ns0:hi>'s Death; and possibly <ns0:hi>Ioab</ns0:hi> might say so for that very reason, that these matters by degrees being known, <ns0:hi>Da<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vid</ns0:hi> might be hardned in Sin, and so <ns0:hi>Ioab</ns0:hi> might have the greater interest in him.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="22">22 So the messenger went and came, and shew<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed David all that Joab had sent him for.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="23">23 And the messenger said unto David, Surely the men prevailed against us, and came out unto us into the field, and we were upon them even unto the entring of the gate <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">We beat them back, and pursued them even to the Gate.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="24">24 And the shooters shot from off the wall upon thy servants, and some of the kings servants be dead, and thy servant Uriah the Hittite is dead also.</ns0:p>

                        </ns0:gap>
                     </ns0:note> dis<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />please thee <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">Be not dejected or discouraged by this sad occasion.</ns0:note>: for the sword devoureth † one as<ns0:note place="margin">‡ <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> So <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
